title: Wildlife and Protected Areas of Assam

blocks.content: Covers Assam's national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, and flagship conservation species — one of the most visually distinctive and consistently tested topics given Assam's globally significant biodiversity.

items: Kaziranga, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed in 1985), is world-renowned as the home of the largest population of the Great Indian One-Horned Rhinoceros, hosting a substantial majority of the world's total population of this species — commonly cited as around two-thirds or more of the global count, though candidates should verify the current census figure against the latest official Kaziranga rhino census before an exam, as these figures are updated periodically.

Beyond rhinos, Kaziranga supports significant populations of wild elephants, wild water buffalo, and tigers (with Kaziranga also recognized as a Tiger Reserve), and is noted for having one of the highest densities of tigers among protected areas in India.

The park is located in the floodplains of the Brahmaputra, spanning parts of Golaghat, Nagaon, and Sonitpur districts, and its ecology is closely tied to the annual flooding cycle of the river, which replenishes its characteristic tall elephant grass and wetland habitats.

Kaziranga has been a long-running conservation success story, with rhino populations recovering substantially from historically low numbers (attributed to hunting and habitat loss in the early 20th century) due to sustained anti-poaching efforts, habitat protection, and programmes like 'Indian Rhino Vision 2020', which also focused on establishing additional rhino populations in other protected areas to reduce over-concentration risk.

The park's four ranges (Kohora/Central, Bagori/Western, Agaratoli/Eastern, and Burapahar/Western extension) are each accessible for wildlife tourism via jeep and, in some ranges, elephant safaris, with the tourist season generally running from November to April (the park is closed during the monsoon flood season).

Manas National Park — a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Tiger Reserve located along the Assam-Bhutan border, known for its rich biodiversity including tigers, elephants, and the endangered pygmy hog and golden langur; Manas was placed on UNESCO's list of World Heritage Sites in Danger for a period during the 1990s–2000s due to conflict-related habitat disturbance, before being removed from that list following successful conservation recovery — a notable and occasionally tested conservation-history fact.
Nameri National Park — known for its birdlife and as a habitat for the white-winged wood duck, among other species; also popular for river-rafting on the Jia Bhoroli river alongside wildlife viewing.

Dibru-Saikhowa National Park — notable for its wetland ecosystem and as a habitat for feral horses (a distinctive and unusual feature for an Indian protected area) and various bird species, located in Upper Assam near the confluence of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries.

Orang National Park — sometimes referred to as a 'mini Kaziranga' due to similar grassland/rhino habitat, located on the northern bank of the Brahmaputra; smaller in area than Kaziranga but ecologically similar.

Assam additionally has several wildlife sanctuaries (a distinct protection category from national parks, generally with a somewhat different management framework) such as Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary, notable for having one of the highest densities of rhinos per unit area of any protected area in the world, despite its comparatively small size.

The Great Indian One-Horned Rhinoceros is the most iconic flagship species associated with Assam; conservation initiatives such as the 'Indian Rhino Vision' programme have focused on securing and expanding rhino populations across multiple protected areas in the state, partly by translocating rhinos from Kaziranga to other parks like Manas and Orang.
The Golden Langur, a rare primate species first formally described relatively recently in scientific terms, is primarily found in the Manas region and parts of western Assam and neighbouring Bhutan.

The Hoolock Gibbon, India's only ape species, is found in the forests of Assam and neighbouring Northeastern states; Assam is home to a dedicated Hoollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary near Jorhat, one of the few protected areas in India specifically established for gibbon conservation.

Assam's wetlands and grasslands support significant avian biodiversity, including several globally threatened bird species; Deepor Beel, a large wetland near Guwahati, is a designated Ramsar site (a wetland of international importance) and an Important Bird Area, frequently tested alongside Kaziranga in wetland/wildlife-focused questions.

cells:
Exam Tip

• Kaziranga's status as home to the world's largest population of the one-horned rhinoceros, and its UNESCO World Heritage Site status, is one of the single most frequently tested facts across all Assam GS exams.

• National park-to-flagship-species matching (Kaziranga-Rhino, Manas-Pygmy hog/Golden langur) is a common question format — build a quick reference table linking each major park to its most distinctive associated species.

• Manas National Park's dual status as both a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a Tiger Reserve, located on the Assam-Bhutan border, is a frequently repeated specific fact.

blocks.content: Q1. Kaziranga National Park is world-renowned for hosting the largest population of which species?
Q2. Which national park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is located along the Assam-Bhutan border?
Q3. The Golden Langur is primarily associated with which region of Assam?
B. Manas region and western Assam
Q4. India's only ape species, found in Assam's forests, is the:
Q5. Kaziranga National Park's ecology is closely tied to the annual flooding cycle of which river?
Q6. Deepor Beel, a wetland near Guwahati, is designated as a:
C. Ramsar site (wetland of international importance)
Q7. Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary is particularly notable for:
A. Having no rhinos at all
B. One of the highest densities of rhinos per unit area in the world
C. Being Assam's largest national park by area
D. Housing the state's only tiger population
Answer: One of the highest densities of rhinos per unit area in the world
